CHAPTER 24 — LIFE PROCESSES - 3: REPRODUCTION

Introduction

Every living organism eventually dies. Yet life on Earth has continued unbroken for billions of years. This continuity is possible only because organisms REPRODUCE — they make new individuals of their own kind before they die. Reproduction is therefore the life process by which a species maintains its CONTINUITY over generations. Unlike nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion — which keep an INDIVIDUAL alive — reproduction is not essential for the survival of the individual organism. Its role is to ensure the survival of the SPECIES. Reproduction also introduces VARIATIONS that, over long periods, help populations adapt to changing environments and drive evolution.

24.1 IMPORTANCE AND TYPES OF REPRODUCTION

Reproduction is important because (a) it ensures the continuity of a species generation after generation; (b) it transmits hereditary characters (the genetic blueprint, DNA) from parents to offspring; and (c) it is a source of variation, which is the raw material for natural selection and evolution.

There are two broad types of reproduction:
 - ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION: a SINGLE parent produces offspring without the formation or fusion of gametes (sex cells). The offspring are genetically IDENTICAL to the parent — they are CLONES. Asexual reproduction is fast and does not need a partner, but it produces little variation.
 - SEXUAL REPRODUCTION: usually TWO parents are involved. Specialised sex cells (GAMETES) — a male gamete and a female gamete — are formed and fuse to form a ZYGOTE. The offspring inherit a mixture of characters from both parents and therefore show VARIATION.

24.2 ASEXUAL REPRODUCTION AND ITS TYPES

In asexual reproduction the new individual arises from a single parent by mitotic cell division, so offspring are genetically identical to the parent. The common methods are:

(a) FISSION — the parent cell splits into new individuals. It is common in unicellular organisms.
   - BINARY FISSION: the parent divides into TWO equal daughter cells. The nucleus divides first, then the cytoplasm. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium and bacteria. In Amoeba the division can occur in any plane; in Paramecium it is transverse; in the malarial parasite Plasmodium, division shows a definite orientation.
   - MULTIPLE FISSION: the parent divides into MANY daughter cells at once. The nucleus divides repeatedly to form many nuclei, each of which is surrounded by cytoplasm, and the parent breaks up into many individuals. Example: Plasmodium (the malarial parasite) and Amoeba under unfavourable conditions (forming a cyst).

(b) BUDDING — a small outgrowth, or BUD, develops on the parent body. The bud grows, develops the features of the parent and finally detaches to lead an independent life. Examples: HYDRA (a multicellular animal — a bud grows on its body, develops a mouth and tentacles, then separates) and YEAST (a unicellular fungus — a small bud pinches off from the parent cell; sometimes a chain of buds forms).

(c) FRAGMENTATION — the body of the organism breaks into TWO OR MORE FRAGMENTS, and each fragment grows into a complete new organism. Example: SPIROGYRA (a filamentous green alga) — the filament breaks into smaller pieces, each of which forms a new filament. Many simple multicellular organisms with relatively undifferentiated body organisation reproduce this way.

(d) REGENERATION — some organisms can regrow lost body parts; if the body is cut into pieces, each piece can regenerate the missing parts to form a complete organism. Example: PLANARIA (flatworm) and Hydra. Regeneration is carried out by specialised cells that proliferate and differentiate. Note: regeneration is not the same as ordinary reproduction, because most organisms cannot reproduce merely by being cut into pieces.

(e) SPORE FORMATION — many fungi and some plants reproduce by producing SPORES — tiny, light, thick-walled reproductive units that can survive unfavourable conditions and germinate into new individuals when conditions are favourable. Example: RHIZOPUS (bread mould) bears tiny upright structures called sporangia (singular: sporangium) on its hyphae; each sporangium contains hundreds of spores. When the sporangium bursts, the spores are dispersed and grow into new mould threads.

(f) VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION — in many plants, new plants arise from VEGETATIVE PARTS (root, stem, leaf) rather than from seeds. The new plants are genetically identical to the parent.
   NATURAL methods:
     - ROOTS: sweet potato, Dahlia (buds on roots grow into new plants).
     - STEMS: potato (eyes/buds on the tuber), ginger and turmeric (rhizomes), onion (bulb), runners of grass.
     - LEAVES: Bryophyllum — buds develop in the notches along the leaf margin and grow into tiny plantlets.
   ARTIFICIAL methods (carried out by humans, especially for crops and ornamental plants):
     - CUTTING: a portion of stem or root with buds is cut and planted; it develops roots and grows into a new plant. Examples: rose, sugarcane, money plant.
     - GRAFTING: the cut stem of one plant (the SCION) is joined to the rooted stem of another plant (the STOCK) so that the tissues unite and grow as one plant. Used in mango, apple and citrus to combine desirable qualities of two plants.
     - LAYERING: a branch of the parent plant is bent to the ground and partly covered with soil; it develops roots while still attached to the parent, and is later separated. Examples: jasmine, lemon, guava.
     - TISSUE CULTURE (micropropagation): small pieces of plant tissue (EXPLANTS) are grown on a nutrient medium under sterile conditions. The tissue forms an undifferentiated mass (CALLUS) which is then induced to form many tiny plantlets. This produces a large number of identical, disease-free plants quickly — used for orchids, ornamental plants and many crops.
   Advantages of vegetative propagation: plants identical to the parent (desirable traits preserved), faster flowering and fruiting, and the ability to grow plants that produce few or no viable seeds (banana, seedless grapes).

24.3 SEXUAL REPRODUCTION — SIGNIFICANCE

In sexual reproduction two gametes — one from each parent — fuse to form a zygote. The gametes are formed by a special type of cell division (meiosis) that halves the chromosome number, so each gamete carries half the genetic material; fertilisation restores the full number. Because the offspring receives a mixture of genes from both parents, it is NOT identical to either parent — sexual reproduction is the main source of VARIATION. Variation gives a population a better chance of surviving changes in the environment and is the basis of evolution by natural selection.

24.4 SEXUAL REPRODUCTION IN FLOWERING PLANTS

The FLOWER is the reproductive organ of a flowering plant. A typical flower has four whorls attached to the swollen tip of the flower stalk (the thalamus):
 - SEPALS (the calyx) — usually green; protect the flower in the bud stage.
 - PETALS (the corolla) — often brightly coloured and scented; attract pollinating insects.
 - STAMENS (the androecium) — the MALE part. Each stamen has a stalk (FILAMENT) bearing an ANTHER. The anther produces POLLEN GRAINS, which contain the male gametes.
 - CARPEL or PISTIL (the gynoecium) — the FEMALE part. It has three regions: the swollen base (OVARY) containing one or more OVULES (each ovule contains the female gamete, the egg); a stalk (STYLE); and a sticky tip (STIGMA) that receives pollen.
A flower with both stamens and carpel is BISEXUAL (e.g. hibiscus, mustard); a flower with only one of them is UNISEXUAL (e.g. papaya, watermelon).

POLLINATION is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma.
 - SELF-POLLINATION: pollen is transferred to the stigma of the same flower (or another flower on the same plant). It does not need an external agent and keeps the parental characters, but gives little variation.
 - CROSS-POLLINATION: pollen is transferred to the stigma of a flower on a DIFFERENT plant of the same species. It needs an agent — wind, water, insects or other animals — and produces variation. Brightly coloured, scented flowers with nectar are adapted for insect pollination.

FERTILISATION: after a pollen grain lands on the stigma, it absorbs nutrients and germinates, producing a POLLEN TUBE that grows down through the style and into the ovule in the ovary. The male gamete travels through the tube and FUSES with the egg (female gamete) inside the ovule to form the ZYGOTE. This fusion of male and female gametes is fertilisation.

After fertilisation:
 - the ZYGOTE develops into the EMBRYO;
 - the OVULE develops into the SEED (which contains the embryo and stored food);
 - the OVARY develops into the FRUIT;
 - the other parts of the flower (sepals, petals, stamens, style, stigma) usually wither and fall off.
When a seed is sown under suitable conditions of water, oxygen and temperature, it GERMINATES — the embryo grows into a new seedling, completing the life cycle.

24.5 REPRODUCTION IN HUMAN BEINGS

Human beings reproduce sexually. The capacity to reproduce develops at PUBERTY (around 10-14 years), when the reproductive organs mature and SECONDARY SEXUAL CHARACTERS appear (e.g. growth of body hair, voice change in boys, breast development and onset of menstruation in girls).

THE MALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM produces male gametes (SPERMS) and delivers them to the female. Its main parts:
 - TESTES (a pair) — lie outside the abdominal cavity in a sac called the SCROTUM, which keeps them at a temperature slightly lower than body temperature (needed for sperm formation). The testes produce sperms and the male hormone TESTOSTERONE.
 - VAS DEFERENS (sperm ducts) — carry sperms from the testes onward.
 - GLANDS (seminal vesicle and prostate) — add fluids to the sperms; the sperms plus these fluids make up the SEMEN.
 - PENIS — the organ that delivers semen into the female reproductive tract.
A sperm is a tiny motile cell with a head (containing the nucleus), a middle piece and a long tail (flagellum) that helps it swim.

THE FEMALE REPRODUCTIVE SYSTEM produces female gametes (EGGS or OVA) and nurtures the developing baby. Its main parts:
 - OVARIES (a pair) — produce eggs (ova) and the female hormones OESTROGEN and PROGESTERONE. At birth a girl's ovaries already contain thousands of immature eggs; from puberty, usually one egg matures and is released about once a month.
 - OVIDUCTS (FALLOPIAN TUBES) — carry the egg from the ovary toward the uterus; fertilisation usually occurs here.
 - UTERUS (womb) — a muscular, pear-shaped organ in which the fertilised egg implants and the baby develops.
 - VAGINA — the passage that receives semen and through which the baby is born.

FERTILISATION AND DEVELOPMENT: during mating, semen is deposited in the vagina and sperms swim up toward the oviduct. If a sperm meets a mature egg there, the two gametes fuse — this is FERTILISATION — forming a single cell, the ZYGOTE. The zygote divides repeatedly to form a ball of cells (the EMBRYO), which moves to the uterus and IMPLANTS in its thick lining. A special tissue, the PLACENTA, connects the developing embryo to the mother's body and supplies it with oxygen and nutrients while removing wastes. The developing baby is now called a FOETUS. Development inside the uterus (GESTATION / pregnancy) takes about NINE MONTHS, after which the baby is born through the vagina (childbirth).

THE MENSTRUAL CYCLE (in brief): from puberty to menopause (around 45-50 years), the female body prepares for a possible pregnancy roughly every 28 days. Each cycle, one egg matures and is released (OVULATION) and the lining of the uterus thickens with blood vessels to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does NOT occur, the egg and the thickened uterine lining are shed through the vagina as blood and tissue — this discharge is MENSTRUATION (the monthly period), lasting 2-5 days. The cycle then begins again.

24.6 REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH

Reproductive health means the complete physical, mental and social well-being related to the reproductive system. Adolescents need correct information and good hygiene to stay healthy.

CONTRACEPTION (birth control, in brief): methods used to prevent unwanted pregnancy and to space or limit births help control population growth and protect the mother's health. The main types are:
 - BARRIER methods — physical barriers that stop sperm from reaching the egg (e.g. condoms, diaphragm). Condoms also help prevent sexually transmitted infections.
 - CHEMICAL / HORMONAL methods — oral pills that change hormone levels so that an egg is not released.
 - INTRA-UTERINE DEVICES (IUDs, e.g. the loop / Copper-T) — placed in the uterus to prevent implantation.
 - SURGICAL methods — vasectomy (in males) and tubectomy (in females) block the tubes that carry the gametes.

SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED DISEASES (STDs, in brief): some diseases spread from person to person through sexual contact. They may be caused by bacteria (e.g. gonorrhoea, syphilis) or viruses (e.g. HIV). HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) causes AIDS (Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome): the virus weakens the body's immune system so the person cannot fight infections. HIV spreads through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood (e.g. shared needles), and from an infected mother to her child. It does NOT spread through ordinary social contact such as shaking hands, sharing food or insect bites. Using condoms, using sterile needles and screening blood before transfusion help prevent its spread. There is no complete cure for AIDS yet, so prevention is the best protection.

SUMMARY

- Reproduction is the life process that ensures the CONTINUITY of a species; it is not needed for an individual's survival but is essential for the species, and it transmits hereditary characters and creates variation.
- ASEXUAL reproduction involves a single parent and produces genetically identical offspring (clones). Its types include fission (binary in Amoeba/Paramecium; multiple in Plasmodium), budding (Hydra, yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Planaria), spore formation (Rhizopus) and vegetative propagation in plants.
- Vegetative propagation can be NATURAL (roots, stems, leaves — e.g. potato, ginger, Bryophyllum) or ARTIFICIAL (cutting, grafting, layering, tissue culture).
- SEXUAL reproduction involves the fusion of two gametes and produces VARIATION.
- In flowering plants, the flower is the reproductive organ; stamens (anther + filament) are male and the carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules) is female. Pollination (self or cross) is followed by fertilisation, after which the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
- In humans, the male system (testes, vas deferens, glands, penis) makes sperms; the female system (ovaries, oviducts, uterus, vagina) makes eggs and nurtures the foetus. The zygote develops in the uterus over about nine months, nourished by the placenta. The menstrual cycle prepares the uterus monthly; menstruation occurs if fertilisation does not happen.
- Reproductive health includes hygiene, contraception (barrier, hormonal, IUD, surgical methods) and protection against STDs such as HIV/AIDS, for which prevention is the key.

chapter_summary.title: Life Processes - 3: Reproduction — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 24. It explains why reproduction ensures the continuity of a species, surveys asexual reproduction and vegetative propagation, describes sexual reproduction in flowering plants and in humans, and introduces reproductive health.

sections.heading: Importance and types of reproduction
bullets: Reproduction is the life process that produces new individuals, ensuring the CONTINUITY of a species across generations.
It is not essential for an individual's survival but is essential for the species; it also transmits hereditary characters (DNA) and creates variation.
Asexual reproduction needs ONE parent and gives genetically identical offspring (clones); sexual reproduction usually needs TWO parents and gives variation.

sections.heading: Asexual reproduction
bullets: FISSION: binary fission gives two daughter cells (Amoeba, Paramecium, bacteria); multiple fission gives many at once (Plasmodium).
BUDDING: a bud grows on the parent and detaches — Hydra (animal) and yeast (fungus).
FRAGMENTATION: the body breaks into pieces that each grow into a new individual — Spirogyra.
REGENERATION: cut pieces regrow the whole organism — Planaria, Hydra.
SPORE FORMATION: thick-walled spores from sporangia germinate into new individuals — Rhizopus (bread mould).

sections.heading: Vegetative propagation in plants
bullets: New plants grow from vegetative parts (root, stem, leaf) and are genetically identical to the parent.
Natural methods: roots (sweet potato), stems (potato eyes, ginger rhizome, onion bulb), leaves (Bryophyllum).
Artificial methods: cutting (rose, sugarcane), grafting (mango, apple — scion on stock), layering (jasmine, guava), tissue culture / micropropagation.
Advantages: desirable parental traits preserved, faster flowering/fruiting, and propagation of seedless plants (banana, grapes).

sections.heading: Sexual reproduction in flowering plants
bullets: The flower is the reproductive organ; its four whorls are sepals, petals, stamens (male) and carpel/pistil (female).
A stamen has a filament and an anther (which makes pollen); a carpel has stigma, style and an ovary containing ovules (each with an egg).
Pollination transfers pollen from anther to stigma — self-pollination (same flower/plant) or cross-pollination (different plant, via wind/water/insects).
After pollination a pollen tube carries the male gamete to the egg; fertilisation forms the zygote. The ovule becomes the SEED and the ovary becomes the FRUIT.

sections.heading: Reproduction in humans and reproductive health
bullets: Male system: testes (in the scrotum) make sperms and testosterone; vas deferens, glands and penis deliver semen.
Female system: ovaries make eggs and hormones; oviducts (where fertilisation occurs), uterus (where the foetus develops) and vagina.
The zygote becomes an embryo, implants in the uterus and develops into a foetus nourished by the placenta over about nine months.
The menstrual cycle (about 28 days) prepares the uterus; menstruation occurs if fertilisation does not happen.
Reproductive health includes hygiene, contraception (barrier, hormonal, IUD, surgical) and protection from STDs such as HIV/AIDS (prevention is key).

key_takeaways: Reproduction ensures the continuity of a species, transmits hereditary characters and is a source of variation.
Asexual reproduction (one parent) gives identical clones: fission, budding, fragmentation, regeneration and spore formation.
Vegetative propagation makes new plants from roots, stems or leaves — naturally or artificially (cutting, grafting, layering, tissue culture).
Sexual reproduction needs two gametes and produces variation that drives adaptation and evolution.
In a flower, stamens are male and the carpel is female; after pollination and fertilisation the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit.
In humans, sperms are made in the testes and eggs in the ovaries; the zygote develops into a foetus in the uterus over about nine months.
Reproductive health covers hygiene, contraception methods and prevention of STDs such as HIV/AIDS.

glossary.definition: The life process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind, ensuring the continuity of the species.
Reproduction involving a single parent and no fusion of gametes; the offspring are genetically identical clones of the parent.
Reproduction involving the formation and fusion of male and female gametes, producing offspring with variation.
Asexual reproduction in which a parent cell divides into two equal daughter cells, as in Amoeba and Paramecium.
Asexual reproduction in which a parent divides simultaneously into many daughter cells, as in the malarial parasite Plasmodium.
Asexual reproduction in which a bud grows on the parent body and later detaches to live independently, as in Hydra and yeast.
Asexual reproduction in which the body breaks into fragments, each of which grows into a new individual, as in Spirogyra.
The ability of some organisms (e.g. Planaria, Hydra) to regrow lost body parts, so that cut pieces can form complete new organisms.
Asexual reproduction by tiny thick-walled spores made in sporangia, which germinate into new individuals, as in Rhizopus.
Production of new plants from vegetative parts (root, stem, leaf), naturally or artificially; offspring are identical to the parent.
The transfer of pollen grains from the anther of a stamen to the stigma of a carpel; it may be self- or cross-pollination.
The fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete to form a zygote.
The single cell formed by the fusion of male and female gametes during fertilisation; it develops into a new individual.
A special tissue connecting the developing embryo/foetus to the mother's uterus, supplying nutrients and oxygen and removing wastes.
The monthly shedding of the unfertilised egg and the thickened uterine lining as blood and tissue when fertilisation does not occur.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Life Processes 3: Reproduction (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 24. Attempt all questions. Draw labelled diagrams where asked.

questions.question: Define reproduction. Why is it called essential for a species but not for an individual?
questions.answer: Reproduction is the life process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind. An individual organism can live its whole life without reproducing — nutrition, respiration, transport and excretion keep it alive. But if no member of a species reproduced, the species would die out when its existing members died. So reproduction is essential for the CONTINUITY OF THE SPECIES, not for the survival of the individual. It also transmits hereditary characters and creates variation.
questions.explanation: Distinguish individual survival (other life processes) from species continuity (reproduction).

questions.question: Distinguish between binary fission and multiple fission, giving one example of each.
questions.answer:
BINARY FISSION: the parent cell divides into TWO equal daughter cells. The nucleus divides first, then the cytoplasm. Example: Amoeba, Paramecium.
MULTIPLE FISSION: the parent divides at once into MANY daughter cells. The nucleus divides repeatedly to form many nuclei, each surrounded by cytoplasm, and the parent breaks up into many individuals. Example: the malarial parasite Plasmodium.
So binary = two offspring; multiple = many offspring from a single division event.
questions.explanation: Two vs many; one nuclear division vs repeated nuclear divisions.

questions.question: Describe budding in Hydra.
questions.answer: Hydra reproduces asexually by budding. A small outgrowth, called a BUD, develops on the side of the parent's body by repeated mitotic cell division. The bud grows and develops a mouth and tentacles like the parent. When fully formed, it DETACHES from the parent body and lives as an independent young Hydra. The new Hydra is genetically identical to the parent.
questions.explanation: Bud forms on body, develops parent features, then detaches.

questions.question: Explain the artificial methods of vegetative propagation: cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture. Give one example of each.
questions.answer:
CUTTING: a piece of stem or root bearing buds is cut and planted in moist soil; it grows roots and develops into a new plant. Example: rose, sugarcane, money plant.
GRAFTING: the cut stem of a desirable plant (the SCION) is joined to the rooted stem of another plant (the STOCK); their tissues unite and grow as a single plant, combining good qualities of both. Example: mango, apple, citrus.
LAYERING: a low branch of the parent plant is bent down and partly covered with soil; it grows roots while still attached to the parent and is later cut off as a new plant. Example: jasmine, lemon, guava.
TISSUE CULTURE (micropropagation): small pieces of plant tissue (explants) are grown on a sterile nutrient medium, forming a callus that develops into many tiny identical plantlets. It produces large numbers of disease-free plants quickly. Example: orchids and many ornamental plants.
All these methods give plants identical to the parent, so desirable traits are preserved.
questions.explanation: Four artificial methods with definitions and examples; note offspring are clones.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of a typical flower and name the male and female reproductive parts and their functions.
questions.answer:
A typical flower has four whorls on the thalamus: SEPALS (calyx) which protect the bud; PETALS (corolla) which attract pollinators; STAMENS (the male part) and the CARPEL/PISTIL (the female part).
MALE PART — STAMEN: made of a stalk (FILAMENT) and an ANTHER. The anther produces POLLEN GRAINS, which contain the male gametes.
FEMALE PART — CARPEL: has three regions — the STIGMA (sticky tip that receives pollen), the STYLE (a stalk), and the OVARY (swollen base) which contains one or more OVULES; each ovule contains the female gamete (egg).
(Labelled diagram: show sepal, petal, filament + anther forming the stamen, and stigma + style + ovary with ovules forming the carpel.)
questions.explanation: Stamen (filament + anther → pollen) is male; carpel (stigma, style, ovary with ovules) is female.

questions.question: Differentiate between self-pollination and cross-pollination.
questions.answer:
SELF-POLLINATION: pollen is transferred from the anther to the stigma of the SAME flower (or another flower on the same plant). No external agent is essential; parental characters are preserved but little variation results.
CROSS-POLLINATION: pollen is transferred to the stigma of a flower on a DIFFERENT plant of the same species. It needs an agent such as wind, water or insects, and produces VARIATION in the offspring.
questions.explanation: Same flower/plant vs different plant; no agent vs agent; less vs more variation.

questions.question: What happens to the ovule and the ovary of a flower after fertilisation?
questions.answer: After fertilisation the ZYGOTE develops into the EMBRYO. The OVULE develops into the SEED (containing the embryo and stored food), and the OVARY develops into the FRUIT, which protects the seeds and may help in their dispersal. The other floral parts (sepals, petals, stamens, style and stigma) usually wither and fall off.
questions.explanation: Ovule → seed; ovary → fruit; zygote → embryo.

questions.question: Describe the human male and female reproductive systems and the role of the placenta.
questions.answer:
MALE SYSTEM: a pair of TESTES lie in the SCROTUM outside the abdomen, where the slightly lower temperature is needed for sperm formation; the testes make SPERMS and the hormone TESTOSTERONE. The VAS DEFERENS carries sperms; glands (seminal vesicle and prostate) add fluid to form SEMEN; the PENIS delivers semen into the female tract.
FEMALE SYSTEM: a pair of OVARIES make EGGS (ova) and the hormones oestrogen and progesterone. The OVIDUCTS (fallopian tubes) carry the egg and are where fertilisation usually occurs. The UTERUS (womb) is where the embryo implants and the baby develops, and the VAGINA receives semen and is the birth canal.
PLACENTA: after the embryo implants in the uterus, the placenta forms to connect the developing baby to the mother. It supplies the foetus with oxygen and nutrients from the mother's blood and removes its wastes (such as carbon dioxide), allowing the foetus to grow over about nine months.
questions.explanation: Male organs (testes, vas deferens, glands, penis), female organs (ovaries, oviducts, uterus, vagina), placenta supplies foetus.

questions.question: What is the menstrual cycle? When does menstruation occur?
questions.answer: The menstrual cycle is the roughly 28-day cycle, from puberty to menopause, in which the female body prepares for a possible pregnancy. Each cycle one egg matures and is released (OVULATION) and the lining of the uterus thickens with blood vessels to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does NOT occur, the unfertilised egg and the thickened uterine lining are shed as blood and tissue through the vagina — this is MENSTRUATION (the monthly period), lasting about 2-5 days. The cycle then repeats.
questions.explanation: Monthly preparation of the uterus; menstruation = shedding of lining when no fertilisation.

questions.question: Name the methods of contraception and explain how HIV/AIDS spreads and how it can be prevented.
questions.answer:
CONTRACEPTION METHODS: (1) Barrier methods (condom, diaphragm) physically stop sperm from reaching the egg; (2) Hormonal methods (oral pills) prevent the release of an egg; (3) Intra-uterine devices (Copper-T) prevent implantation; (4) Surgical methods (vasectomy in males, tubectomy in females) block the tubes carrying the gametes.
HIV/AIDS: HIV is a virus that weakens the immune system, causing AIDS. It SPREADS through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood (e.g. shared needles or unscreened transfusion), and from an infected mother to her baby. It does NOT spread by shaking hands, sharing food or insect bites. PREVENTION: use condoms, use sterile needles, screen blood before transfusion, and spread awareness — since there is no complete cure, prevention is the best protection.
questions.explanation: Four contraception types; HIV routes of spread and prevention measures.

questions.question: State two reasons why reproduction is important.
questions.answer: (1) It ensures the CONTINUITY OF THE SPECIES — new individuals replace those that die. (2) It transmits hereditary characters from parents to offspring and is a source of VARIATION, which helps populations adapt and evolve.
questions.explanation: Continuity of species + transmission of characters/variation.

questions.question: Give three differences between asexual and sexual reproduction.
questions.answer:
(1) Number of parents: asexual needs ONE parent; sexual usually needs TWO.
(2) Gametes: no gametes are formed/fused in asexual reproduction; sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes.
(3) Variation: asexual offspring are genetically IDENTICAL (clones); sexual offspring show VARIATION.
questions.explanation: Parents, gametes and variation distinguish the two types.

questions.question: What is binary fission? Give one example.
questions.answer: Binary fission is a type of asexual reproduction in which a single parent cell divides into TWO equal daughter cells; the nucleus divides first, followed by the cytoplasm. Example: Amoeba (also Paramecium and bacteria).
questions.explanation: Division into two; example Amoeba.

questions.question: Describe spore formation in Rhizopus.
questions.answer: Rhizopus (bread mould) develops upright thread-like structures bearing tiny knob-like SPORANGIA on its hyphae. Each sporangium contains hundreds of tiny, thick-walled SPORES. When the sporangium bursts, the spores are released and dispersed; under favourable conditions each spore germinates into a new mould.
questions.explanation: Sporangia produce spores that germinate into new individuals.

questions.question: How does fragmentation help Spirogyra reproduce?
questions.answer: Spirogyra is a filamentous green alga. Its filament breaks (fragments) into two or more smaller pieces, either by chance or in unfavourable handling. Each fragment then grows by cell division into a complete new filament. Thus a single parent filament gives rise to several new individuals.
questions.explanation: Filament breaks; each fragment regrows into a filament.

questions.question: Name the type of asexual reproduction in: (i) Hydra, (ii) Planaria, (iii) yeast, (iv) Plasmodium.
questions.answer:
(i) Hydra – budding.
(ii) Planaria – regeneration.
(iii) yeast – budding.
(iv) Plasmodium – multiple fission.
questions.explanation: Match each organism to its asexual mode.

questions.question: Why are spores useful to organisms like Rhizopus?
questions.answer: Spores are tiny, light and thick-walled. Being light, they are easily DISPERSED by air to new places. Their thick protective wall lets them SURVIVE unfavourable conditions (such as dryness or lack of food). When conditions become favourable, each spore germinates into a new individual. Thus spores aid both dispersal and survival.
questions.explanation: Light for dispersal; thick wall for survival.

questions.question: Distinguish between budding and fragmentation.
questions.answer:
BUDDING: a small outgrowth (BUD) develops on the parent body, grows to resemble the parent and then DETACHES to live independently. Example: Hydra, yeast.
FRAGMENTATION: the body of the organism BREAKS into two or more fragments and each fragment grows into a complete new organism. Example: Spirogyra.
So budding starts from a single outgrowth on a living parent, while fragmentation involves the breaking up of the parent body itself.
questions.explanation: Outgrowth that detaches vs body breaking into pieces.

questions.question: Why is regeneration not regarded as the normal mode of reproduction in most animals?
questions.answer: Regeneration is the ability to regrow lost body parts and is well developed only in a few simple animals (e.g. Planaria, Hydra). Most complex animals can repair small injuries but CANNOT form a whole new organism if cut into pieces. Therefore, although regeneration produces new individuals in some organisms, it is not the usual or general way most animals reproduce.
questions.explanation: Only some simple animals fully regenerate; most cannot.

questions.question: State two advantages and one disadvantage of asexual reproduction.
questions.answer:
Advantages: (1) It is FAST — many offspring can be produced quickly. (2) It needs only ONE parent, so no partner is required and it works well when organisms are isolated or conditions are stable.
Disadvantage: it produces little or NO VARIATION — offspring are genetically identical clones, so if the environment changes unfavourably, the whole population is equally vulnerable.
questions.explanation: Fast and single-parent, but little variation.

questions.question: Define vegetative propagation and give two examples of plants propagated this way.
questions.answer: Vegetative propagation is the type of asexual reproduction in plants in which new plants develop from VEGETATIVE PARTS (root, stem or leaf) rather than from seeds; the new plants are identical to the parent. Examples: potato (stem tuber), Bryophyllum (leaf), ginger (rhizome), rose (stem cutting).
questions.explanation: New plants from vegetative parts; identical to parent.

questions.question: Explain the difference between grafting and layering.
questions.answer:
GRAFTING: the cut stem of one plant (the SCION, chosen for good fruit or flowers) is joined to the rooted stem of another plant (the STOCK, chosen for strong roots). Their tissues unite and grow as one plant. Example: mango, apple.
LAYERING: a low branch of the parent plant is bent to the ground and partly buried in soil; it develops roots WHILE STILL ATTACHED to the parent, and is later separated as a new plant. Example: jasmine, guava.
Thus grafting joins two different plants, while layering uses a branch of the same plant to form roots.
questions.explanation: Grafting joins scion+stock; layering roots an attached branch.

questions.question: What is tissue culture? State one advantage.
questions.answer: Tissue culture (micropropagation) is a method of producing new plants by growing small pieces of plant tissue (explants) on a sterile nutrient medium; the tissue forms a callus that develops into many tiny plantlets. Advantage: a very LARGE NUMBER of identical, disease-free plants can be produced quickly in a small space, irrespective of the season.
questions.explanation: Growing plants from tissue on nutrient medium; many disease-free clones.

questions.question: State two advantages of vegetative propagation over reproduction by seeds.
questions.answer: (1) The new plants are genetically IDENTICAL to the parent, so the desirable qualities of the parent (e.g. taste, colour, disease resistance) are preserved exactly. (2) It allows the growing of plants that produce few or NO viable seeds, such as banana, seedless grapes and orange; it also gives faster flowering and fruiting.
questions.explanation: Preserves parental traits; grows seedless plants; faster fruiting.

questions.question: A gardener wants all his apple trees to bear the same sweet fruit as one prized tree. Which method should he use and why?
questions.answer: He should use a VEGETATIVE method such as GRAFTING (or cutting). Because vegetative propagation produces plants genetically IDENTICAL to the parent, every new tree will bear exactly the same sweet fruit as the prized tree. If he grew the trees from seeds (sexual reproduction), variation would make the fruit differ from the parent. Grafting the scion of the prized tree onto rootstocks gives many identical trees.
questions.explanation: Grafting/cutting gives identical clones, preserving the prized fruit quality.

questions.question: Name the parts of a stamen and a carpel.
questions.answer:
STAMEN (male part): made of a stalk called the FILAMENT and a knob called the ANTHER (which produces pollen grains).
CARPEL/PISTIL (female part): made of the STIGMA (sticky top that receives pollen), the STYLE (a stalk), and the OVARY (swollen base containing ovules).
questions.explanation: Stamen = filament + anther; carpel = stigma + style + ovary.

questions.question: Describe how fertilisation occurs in a flower.
questions.answer: After a pollen grain lands on the stigma (pollination), it germinates and produces a POLLEN TUBE. The pollen tube grows down through the style and into the ovule inside the ovary. The MALE GAMETE travels down the tube and FUSES with the EGG (female gamete) inside the ovule. This fusion of male and female gametes is FERTILISATION, and it forms the ZYGOTE, which develops into the embryo.
questions.explanation: Pollen tube carries male gamete to egg; their fusion = fertilisation.

questions.question: What changes occur in a flower after fertilisation?
questions.answer: After fertilisation: the ZYGOTE becomes the EMBRYO; the OVULE becomes the SEED; the OVARY becomes the FRUIT. The remaining parts of the flower — sepals, petals, stamens, style and stigma — usually wither and fall off.
questions.explanation: Ovule→seed, ovary→fruit, zygote→embryo; other parts fall off.

questions.question: What is meant by germination of a seed?
questions.answer: Germination is the process in which a seed, sown under suitable conditions of water, oxygen (air) and a suitable temperature, begins to grow. The EMBRYO inside the seed uses the stored food, develops a tiny root and shoot, and grows into a new seedling, thus completing the life cycle.
questions.explanation: Embryo in the seed grows into a seedling under suitable conditions.

questions.question: Why does cross-pollination need an external agent while self-pollination usually does not?
questions.answer: In self-pollination, pollen only has to reach the stigma of the SAME flower (or another flower on the same plant), which can happen by the flower's own structure without help. In cross-pollination, pollen must travel to a flower on a DIFFERENT plant, often some distance away, so it needs a CARRYING AGENT such as wind, water or an animal (e.g. insect) to transfer the pollen.
questions.explanation: Pollen must travel between plants in cross-pollination, requiring an agent.

questions.question: How are insect-pollinated flowers adapted to attract insects?
questions.answer: Insect-pollinated flowers usually have BRIGHTLY COLOURED petals and a sweet SCENT to attract insects from a distance, and they often produce sugary NECTAR as a food reward. Their pollen is usually sticky or spiny so that it clings to the insect's body and is carried to another flower. These features make insect pollination effective.
questions.explanation: Colour, scent, nectar and sticky pollen attract and use insects.

questions.question: Which type of pollination is better for the long-term survival of a species and why?
questions.answer: CROSS-POLLINATION is generally better for long-term survival. Because it mixes genes from two different parent plants, it produces OFFSPRING WITH VARIATION. Variation increases the chance that some individuals will survive changes in the environment, disease or new conditions, helping the species adapt and evolve. Self-pollination keeps characters fixed but offers little variation, so a population is more vulnerable to change.
questions.explanation: Cross-pollination gives variation, aiding adaptation and survival.

questions.question: Name the main parts of the human male reproductive system and state the function of the testes.
questions.answer: Main parts: TESTES (a pair, in the scrotum), VAS DEFERENS (sperm ducts), associated GLANDS (seminal vesicle and prostate), and the PENIS. Function of the testes: they produce the male gametes (SPERMS) and the male hormone TESTOSTERONE.
questions.explanation: Testes, vas deferens, glands, penis; testes make sperms and testosterone.

questions.question: Name the main parts of the human female reproductive system and state the function of the ovaries.
questions.answer: Main parts: OVARIES (a pair), OVIDUCTS (fallopian tubes), UTERUS (womb) and VAGINA. Function of the ovaries: they produce the female gametes (EGGS / ova) and the female hormones (oestrogen and progesterone).
questions.explanation: Ovaries, oviducts, uterus, vagina; ovaries make eggs and hormones.

questions.question: Trace the path of development from a fertilised egg to a baby in humans.
questions.answer: Fertilisation of the egg by a sperm in the oviduct forms a single cell, the ZYGOTE. The zygote divides repeatedly to form a ball of cells, the EMBRYO. The embryo moves to the UTERUS and IMPLANTS in its thick lining. The PLACENTA develops to supply the growing baby with oxygen and nutrients and remove its wastes. The developing baby (now a FOETUS) grows in the uterus for about NINE MONTHS, after which it is born through the vagina.
questions.explanation: Zygote→embryo→implants in uterus→foetus nourished by placenta→born after ~9 months.

questions.question: What is the role of the placenta?
questions.answer: The placenta is a special tissue that connects the developing embryo/foetus to the wall of the mother's uterus. It allows oxygen and nutrients to pass from the mother's blood to the foetus, and waste products (such as carbon dioxide) to pass from the foetus back to the mother for removal. Thus it nourishes the foetus and removes its wastes during pregnancy.
questions.explanation: It supplies the foetus with nutrients/oxygen and removes its wastes.

questions.question: What is the menstrual cycle and why does menstruation occur?
questions.answer: The menstrual cycle is the roughly 28-day cycle in which the female body prepares for a possible pregnancy: an egg matures and is released (ovulation) and the uterine lining thickens to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does NOT occur, the unfertilised egg and the thickened lining are shed as blood and tissue through the vagina — this shedding is called MENSTRUATION. It marks that pregnancy has not occurred, and the cycle then begins again.
questions.explanation: Monthly preparation of the uterus; lining shed when no fertilisation.

questions.question: What is meant by reproductive health?
questions.answer: Reproductive health means a state of complete PHYSICAL, MENTAL and SOCIAL well-being in all matters relating to the reproductive system and its functions. It includes proper hygiene, correct information about reproduction, prevention of sexually transmitted diseases, and the ability to make safe and informed decisions about reproduction.
questions.explanation: Complete physical, mental and social well-being of the reproductive system.

questions.question: List the main methods of contraception with one example of each.
questions.answer:
(1) BARRIER methods — a physical barrier stops sperm reaching the egg; example: condom, diaphragm.
(2) HORMONAL methods — change hormone levels to prevent the release of an egg; example: oral contraceptive pills.
(3) INTRA-UTERINE DEVICES (IUDs) — placed in the uterus to prevent implantation; example: Copper-T.
(4) SURGICAL methods — block the tubes carrying gametes; example: vasectomy (male), tubectomy (female).
questions.explanation: Barrier, hormonal, IUD and surgical methods with examples.

questions.question: How does HIV/AIDS spread and how can it be prevented?
questions.answer:
SPREAD: HIV spreads through (1) unprotected sexual contact with an infected person, (2) transfer of infected BLOOD — for example, sharing needles or transfusion of unscreened blood, and (3) from an infected MOTHER to her baby during pregnancy, birth or breast-feeding. It does NOT spread by ordinary social contact such as shaking hands, sharing food or insect bites.
PREVENTION: use condoms, use only sterile/disposable needles, screen blood before transfusion, and create awareness. Since there is no complete cure, prevention is the best protection.
questions.explanation: Sexual contact, infected blood, mother-to-child; prevented by condoms, sterile needles, screened blood.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

All living organisms eventually die, yet their species continue for millions of years because they reproduce. Some organisms reproduce from a single parent, while others need two parents and special sex cells.

(i) Why is reproduction essential for a species but not for an individual?
(ii) Name the two main types of reproduction.
(iii) Which type produces clones?
(iv) Which type is the main source of variation?
questions.answer:
(i) An individual can survive without reproducing, but if no member of a species reproduced, the species would die out when its members died. So reproduction maintains the CONTINUITY OF THE SPECIES, not the individual's survival.
(ii) Asexual reproduction and sexual reproduction.
(iii) Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical offspring (clones).
(iv) Sexual reproduction is the main source of variation.
questions.explanation: Species continuity, the two types, clones (asexual) and variation (sexual).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Unicellular and simple organisms use several methods of asexual reproduction. Amoeba splits into two; Plasmodium splits into many; yeast forms a bud; and Rhizopus releases spores.

(i) Name the method used by Amoeba.
(ii) Name the method used by Plasmodium.
(iii) How does yeast reproduce?
(iv) Name the structures in which Rhizopus makes its spores.
questions.answer:
(i) Binary fission (the parent divides into two daughter cells).
(ii) Multiple fission (the parent divides into many daughter cells at once).
(iii) Yeast reproduces by BUDDING — a small bud grows on the parent cell and pinches off.
(iv) Sporangia (each sporangium contains many spores).
questions.explanation: Binary fission, multiple fission, budding and sporangia.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Hydra and yeast both reproduce by budding, but they are very different organisms. Planaria, when cut into pieces, can regrow into several whole worms.

(i) How does a bud finally become a new individual in Hydra?
(ii) State one difference between Hydra and yeast.
(iii) Name the process by which Planaria forms whole worms from pieces.
(iv) Why is this process not called the normal mode of reproduction?
questions.answer:
(i) The bud grows on the parent's body, develops a mouth and tentacles like the parent, and then DETACHES to live as an independent young Hydra.
(ii) Hydra is a MULTICELLULAR animal, while yeast is a UNICELLULAR fungus.
(iii) Regeneration.
(iv) Because most organisms CANNOT reproduce merely by being cut into pieces — only a few simple animals can regenerate fully — so it is not the usual mode of reproduction.
questions.explanation: Budding in Hydra, Hydra vs yeast, regeneration, and why regeneration is special.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A nursery owner wants to quickly produce many identical plants of a prized rose and a prized mango variety. He has learnt about cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture.

(i) Which simple method suits the rose, using a piece of its stem?
(ii) Which method joins a scion of the prized mango to a strong rootstock?
(iii) Which method can quickly produce thousands of identical disease-free plantlets in the lab?
(iv) Why will all the new plants resemble the parent?
questions.answer:
(i) Cutting — a piece of rose stem with buds is planted and grows roots into a new plant.
(ii) Grafting — the scion (prized mango shoot) is joined to a strong rootstock (stock).
(iii) Tissue culture (micropropagation) — tiny tissue pieces grown on a nutrient medium form many identical plantlets.
(iv) Because all these are VEGETATIVE (asexual) methods, the new plants are genetically IDENTICAL clones of the parent, so they keep the parent's desirable traits.
questions.explanation: Cutting, grafting, tissue culture, and why offspring are identical clones.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A flower is the reproductive organ of a flowering plant. It has male and female parts. After pollen reaches the stigma, a series of events leads to the formation of seeds and fruits.

(i) Name the male and female reproductive parts of a flower.
(ii) Where are the pollen grains and the ovules produced?
(iii) What is the structure that carries the male gamete to the egg?
(iv) What do the ovule and the ovary become after fertilisation?
questions.answer:
(i) The male part is the STAMEN; the female part is the CARPEL (pistil).
(ii) Pollen grains are produced in the ANTHER of the stamen; ovules are produced in the OVARY of the carpel.
(iii) The POLLEN TUBE, which grows from the germinating pollen grain down the style to the ovule.
(iv) The ovule becomes the SEED and the ovary becomes the FRUIT.
questions.explanation: Stamen/carpel, anther/ovary, pollen tube, and ovule→seed, ovary→fruit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In some plants pollen reaches the stigma of the same flower; in others it is carried to a flower on a different plant by wind or insects. Brightly coloured, scented flowers are usually visited by insects.

(i) Name the two types of pollination.
(ii) Which type needs an external agent?
(iii) Give two adaptations of insect-pollinated flowers.
(iv) Which type of pollination produces more variation, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Self-pollination and cross-pollination.
(ii) Cross-pollination needs an external agent (wind, water or insects).
(iii) Bright colour and sweet scent (and nectar) to attract insects; sticky pollen that clings to the insect's body.
(iv) Cross-pollination produces more variation, because the pollen comes from a DIFFERENT plant, mixing genes from two parents.
questions.explanation: Two pollination types, agent need, insect adaptations, and variation in cross-pollination.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In humans, sperms made in the testes are deposited in the female tract and swim toward the oviduct. If a sperm meets a mature egg, fertilisation occurs and a new life begins.

(i) Where are sperms and eggs produced?
(ii) Where does fertilisation usually take place?
(iii) What is the fertilised egg called, and where does it develop?
(iv) Roughly how long does human pregnancy last?
questions.answer:
(i) Sperms are produced in the TESTES; eggs (ova) are produced in the OVARIES.
(ii) Fertilisation usually takes place in the OVIDUCT (fallopian tube).
(iii) The fertilised egg is called the ZYGOTE; it develops (as an embryo and then a foetus) in the UTERUS.
(iv) About NINE MONTHS.
questions.explanation: Testes/ovaries, oviduct, zygote in uterus, and ~9 months gestation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

From puberty to menopause, the female body follows a roughly 28-day cycle. Each cycle an egg matures and the uterine lining thickens to prepare for pregnancy.

(i) What is the release of a mature egg called?
(ii) Why does the uterine lining thicken each cycle?
(iii) What happens to the lining if fertilisation does not occur?
(iv) What is this monthly discharge called?
questions.answer:
(i) Ovulation.
(ii) The lining thickens with blood vessels so that it is ready to receive and nourish a fertilised egg if pregnancy occurs.
(iii) If fertilisation does NOT occur, the unfertilised egg and the thickened lining break down and are shed as blood and tissue through the vagina.
(iv) Menstruation (the monthly period).
questions.explanation: Ovulation, why the lining thickens, shedding when no fertilisation, and menstruation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Reproductive health includes protection from sexually transmitted diseases and the responsible use of contraception. HIV/AIDS is a serious viral STD for which there is no complete cure.

(i) Give one barrier and one surgical method of contraception.
(ii) Which contraceptive also helps prevent STDs?
(iii) State two ways HIV spreads.
(iv) State two ways to prevent the spread of HIV.
questions.answer:
(i) Barrier method: condom (or diaphragm). Surgical method: vasectomy (male) or tubectomy (female).
(ii) The condom — being a barrier, it also blocks the pathogens that cause STDs.
(iii) Through unprotected sexual contact, through infected blood (e.g. shared needles or unscreened transfusion), and from an infected mother to her baby (any two).
(iv) Use condoms; use only sterile/disposable needles; screen blood before transfusion; spread awareness (any two).
questions.explanation: Contraception types, condom for STDs, HIV spread routes and prevention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A community health worker is teaching teenagers that AIDS cannot be cured and that many myths exist about how it spreads. She stresses that prevention is the only reliable protection.

(i) Name the virus that causes AIDS.
(ii) State one common MYTH about how HIV spreads, and correct it.
(iii) Why is prevention stressed rather than cure?
(iv) Suggest two preventive measures a teenager should know.
questions.answer:
(i) HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus).
(ii) Myth: that HIV spreads by shaking hands, sharing food or insect bites. Correction: HIV does NOT spread through such ordinary social contact; it spreads mainly through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood and from mother to child.
(iii) Because there is no complete cure for AIDS yet, so stopping the spread (prevention) is the only reliable way to protect people.
(iv) Use condoms during sexual contact; never share needles/use only sterile needles; ensure blood is screened before transfusion; spread correct awareness (any two).
questions.explanation: HIV, correcting a spread myth, why prevention matters, and preventive measures.
